title: Unitary and semigroup representations

slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: An ordered spectral gap permits a Sylvester equation to be solved by integrating decaying exponentials.
body: For interlaced but separated spectra, the differences do not all share a sign, so we need a different construction. We study a related construction that works when the spectra are separated but their differences may have either sign. The key change is to use unitary groups: exponentials with an imaginary unit in the exponent. These produce oscillations rather than decay. Then a scalar Fourier multiplier will turn each oscillation back into the reciprocal of its spectral difference.

slides.title: The Sylvester orbit
slides.lead: Let A and B be bounded self-adjoint operators on complex Hilbert spaces.
body: Let C be a bounded map from the space on which B acts into the space on which A acts. For each real time t, define an operator U of t by exponentiating i times t times A. Define V of t using B the same way. Because the generators are self-adjoint, U and V are unitary: they preserve lengths and have their adjoints as inverses. Now transport C by applying U of t on the left and the inverse of V of t on the right. Call the result F of t. At time zero, both unitary maps are identities, so F of zero equals C. At any other time, F describes how C looks after a left and right unitary evolution.

slides.title: Check the orbit in diagonal coordinates
slides.lead: Assume for the moment that A and B are diagonal, with real eigenvalues a and b in the corresponding positions.
body: On the matrix entry joining a to b, left unitary evolution multiplies by the exponential of i t a. Right inverse evolution multiplies by the exponential of negative i t b. The product is the exponential of i t times a minus b. Each matrix coefficient therefore oscillates with frequency equal to its spectral difference. Different entries can oscillate clockwise or counterclockwise depending on the sign of the difference. Unlike the ordered semigroup, there is no single exponential decay envelope.

slides.title: A scalar reciprocal multiplier
slides.lead: Suppose every absolute difference between a spectral value of A and one of B is at least a positive number delta.
body: We want an integrable complex-valued function of time, call it mu, with this property: integrate mu of t times the exponential of i t omega over all real times, and the result is one over omega whenever the absolute value of omega is at least delta. Think of the time variable as an input to the Fourier transform. We prescribe the transform of mu away from a forbidden interval around zero. Inside that interval, we have freedom, because no spectral difference we need to invert can occur there. That freedom matters.

slides.title: Build the operator inverse
slides.lead: Return to the operator orbit of C.
body: Multiply it by mu of t and integrate over all real t. Call the resulting operator Y. In diagonal coordinates, the entry of Y joining eigenvalues a and b is the entry of C times the integral of mu of t times the exponential of i t times a minus b. The multiplier property evaluates this integral as one divided by a minus b. Therefore the entry of Y is the entry of C divided by the spectral difference. We have reconstructed the unique entrywise Sylvester solution. This is more than a compact notation for the finite calculation. The expression is basis independent, and its integrand is defined directly in the space of bounded operators.

slides.title: Why the infinite-dimensional argument needs care
slides.lead: In finite dimensions we checked every coefficient in eigenbases.
body: But a bounded self-adjoint operator on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space may have continuous spectrum and no orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. We cannot write an entrywise sum over eigenvalues and pretend it still covers every operator. Instead, the spectral theorem lets us approximate each self-adjoint operator by a finite spectral step operator: a finite linear combination of spectral projections, with coefficients chosen from the original spectrum. For these finite spectral steps, the multiplier identity applies block by block. The approximations converge in operator norm.

slides.title: How the semigroup and unitary methods differ
slides.lead: Let us compare the two integral constructions.
body: When A is entirely above B by delta, the semigroup integrand decays as the exponential of negative delta times time. We integrate only over nonnegative times, and the mass of the scalar envelope is one over delta. For general pairwise-separated spectra, some spectral differences are positive and others negative. A single decaying semigroup cannot treat them all. The unitary representation works with both signs by oscillating over all real times and inserting a Fourier multiplier. The multiplier's absolute mass produces pi over two delta.

slides.title: An example with both signs
slides.lead: Let A be diagonal with entries negative one and positive one, and B the one-dimensional zero operator.
body: Let C be the column with entries two and three. The spectral differences are negative one and positive one, so delta equals one. The Sylvester solution has entries negative two and positive three. For the first coefficient, the unitary orbit oscillates with frequency negative one; for the second, with frequency positive one. The scalar multiplier returns negative one for the first reciprocal and positive one for the second, producing exactly the required signs. No single choice of positive-time exponential decay using the same orientation can handle both entries.

slides.title: The generator viewpoint
body: The maps sending X to U of t X V of negative t form a one-parameter unitary group on the Hilbert space of Hilbert–Schmidt operators. Its generator is multiplication by i times the Sylvester operator. In that Hilbert–Schmidt setting, the entire spectral calculation can be understood as functional calculus for a self-adjoint generator. This will later yield a sharper estimate in the square-summable operator norm. For now, reconstruct the derivative of the orbit, verify the opposite-frequency example, and derive the norm estimate from the integral's absolute majorant.

slides.title: The mathematical relationship
body: The maps sending X to U of t X V of negative t form a one-parameter unitary group on the Hilbert space of Hilbert–Schmidt operators. Its generator is multiplication by i times the Sylvester operator.

slides.title: What to retain
slides.lead: Those steps prepare us for another solution method that does not require self-adjointness at all: contour integration of resolvents.
